The benchmark material is the same in both studies, and the capacity endpoint is the same, so the difference in reported lifetime is carried by the duty cycle rather than by the material or by the endpoint. Cycling is the harsher condition: each regeneration repeats the thermal and mechanical stress that steady duty applies once, and a lifetime measured under cycling is expected to fall short of a lifetime measured at steady load even where the material is unchanged. The studies also agree on the point that matters for the comparison: neither reports a change in the material itself across the testing, and neither attributes the lifetime reached to a difference in the endpoint adopted. The disagreement is therefore a disagreement about duty, reported as a disagreement about lifetime, and it is resolved only by matching the duty to the service the material will actually perform. On that basis the preference here is limited. Where the intended service cycles the material, the cycled values are the ones to design against, because the steady-load values were obtained under a duty the material will not see. Where the service holds a steady load, the preference reverses.
